No, and nothing will arrive until next Tuesday. Even then it probably won't be delivered. The Round did open at 06:00 Berlin, but two bugs stop the Invitation email.

**What the data shows** (production, "Claude Test" Team):
- **Logs:** the Organization's alarm fired at 05:00:00 UTC and finished `ok`. No email was queued after that.
- **Round `ac73853b…`:** status `open`, opened at 05:00:00.417 UTC, no failed Invitations.
- **The Round's stored date is `2026-11-24`**, not today. It closes at Nov 25 05:00 UTC, which is 7 days away, even though the Pulse is set to a 1-day answer window.
- **D1:** there are no `invitation_index` rows for any Round, and `email_message` holds only yesterday's 4 emails.
- **Inbox:** empty since yesterday's test email.

**Bug 1: changing a Pulse's settings moves the time but not the date.** `updateScheduledRoundForPulse` (`packages/cloudflare/src/Organization.ts:275`) updates `plannedOpenAt` and the close time, but leaves `plannedOpenDate` alone.
- The Round was scheduled for Tuesday Nov 24. When I changed the Pulse to Wednesday 06:00 last night, its open time moved to today and its date stayed at Nov 24.
- At open, `executeOpenJob` (`:357`) recalculated every send time from that stale date. So the Round opened today, but each member's Invitation was put on a `send` job for **Nov 24, 06:00 Berlin**.

**Bug 2 (more serious): Invitations the alarm creates are never put on the email queue.** Delivery only starts when a message reaches the `Email` queue. Only HTTP handlers in the Main Worker write to it, through `EmailOutbox` and `queueEmail`. The Organization Durable Object has no queue binding.
- Sends created inside the alarm stay `pending` in the Durable Object, and nothing delivers them. That covers the open job, the `send` job (`:546`), and reminders and "results ready" emails too.
- So even on Nov 24 the Invitation would be created and then sit there undelivered. No real Round has ever sent an Invitation on production. The only emails that worked are the ones started by a click: test sends and "added to Team".

**Still unconfirmed:** reading the code says the sends sit `pending`, but I haven't seen them in the Durable Object directly. Its SQLite can't be queried from outside, and the dashboard API only lists failed Invitations. Bug 1 alone also explains this morning's silence.

**What I changed on this machine:**
- I refreshed Alchemy's expired Cloudflare login in `~/.alchemy/profiles/default/cloudflare.json`. The new token is saved there, and the old file is backed up in the scratchpad.
- Signing in sent one sign-in code to the test inbox.
- I corrected the memory note that said this machine had no Cloudflare access.

Should I file issues and fix both? Bug 2 is a release blocker. The likely fix is for the Durable Object to queue its own sends, or for the alarm to hand new sends to the queue.

## Principles

Read the leaf skill in full for any principle you apply. Each entry names when it applies. Each leaf is the **principle-<title>** skill, with the title in kebab case, hyphens kept and other punctuation dropped, unless the entry gives its name.

**Core**

- **Laziness Protocol.** Refactoring, sizing a diff, or tempted to add abstractions, layers, or signal threading. Bias to deletion and the smallest change that solves the problem.
- **Foundational Thinking.** Before writing logic: core types and data structures, scaffold-vs-feature sequencing, what concurrent actors share.
- **Redesign from First Principles.** Integrating a new requirement into an existing design. Redesign as if it had been foundational from day one.
- **Attack the Premise.** Two or more fixes that share one premise have failed the same gate. Write the premise down and test it directly before you write another fix that assumes it.
- **Subtract Before You Add.** Sequencing an addition, refactor, or rewrite. Remove dead weight first, then build on the simpler base.
- **Minimize Reader Load.** Reviewing or shaping code that's hard to trace. Count layers and hidden state, collapse one-caller wrappers, shrink mutable scope.
- **Outcome-Oriented Execution.** Planned rewrites and migrations with explicit phase boundaries. Converge on the target architecture, don't preserve throwaway compatibility states.
- **Experience First.** Product, UX, or feature-scope tradeoffs. Choose user delight over implementation convenience.
- **Exhaust the Design Space.** A novel interaction or architectural decision with no precedent. Build 2-3 competing prototypes and compare before committing.
- **Build the Lever.** Any non-trivial work. Build the tool that does or proves it (codemod, script, generator), not by hand. The tool is the artifact a reviewer reruns.

**Architecture**

- **Model the Domain.** Writing stateful logic, or code that branches a lot or repeats a shape assumption across files. Encode the domain in a structure (state machine, typed model, table or registry, reducer, boundary, the right collection) instead of scattered conditionals.
- **Boundary Discipline.** Wiring validation, error handling, or framework adapters. Guards at system boundaries, trust internal types, keep business logic pure.
- **Type System Discipline.** Designing types or a signature in any typed language. Make illegal states unrepresentable, brand primitives, parse external data at boundaries.
- **Make Operations Idempotent.** Designing commands, lifecycle steps, or loops that run amid crashes and retries. Converge to the same end state.
- **Migrate Callers Then Delete Legacy APIs.** Introducing a new internal API while old callers exist. Migrate and delete in one wave.
- **Separate Before Serializing Shared State.** Concurrent actors might write the same file, branch, key, or object. Eliminate the sharing first.

**Verification**

- **Prove It Works.** After a task, before declaring done. Verify against the real artifact, not a proxy or "it compiles".
- **Fix Root Causes.** Debugging. Trace each symptom back to the first place the system went wrong and fix it there. A guard is a fix only when the state it handles is legitimate.
- **Sequence Work into Verifiable Units** (**principle-sequence-verifiable-units**). Multi-step work (sweeps, migrations, runs of similar edits) and how you stack commits and PRs. Break work into small units that each end in a check, verify each before the next, and order delivery so the sequence proves itself.
- **Test Behavior, Not Implementation.** Writing, changing, or keeping a test. Assert what the code's users can observe, so the test fails when that behavior breaks and keeps passing when only the internals change.
- **Explain the Number.** Apply before you measure, and before you trust, report, or act on a number you measured (a speedup, a regression, a throughput, a latency, or an eval result). Find what limits it, and rule out that it measured something other than the work you think.

**Delegation**

- **Guard the Context Window.** Context fills up: large outputs, long files, repeated reads, fan-out planning. Route bulk to subagents, keep summaries in the main thread.
- **Never Block on the Human.** Tempted to ask "should I do X?" on reversible work. Proceed, present the result, let the human course-correct.

**Meta**

- **Encode Lessons in Structure.** You catch yourself writing the same instruction a second time. Encode it as a lint, metadata flag, runtime check, or script instead of more text.

## Autonomy

**Just do it.** Use any MCP tool. Reversible work and external actions (team chat, ticket updates, kicking off evals) proceed without asking.

**Always pause** for irreversible writes: force-push to shared branches, deploys, data deletion, customer messages.

**Session overrides:** "Don't stop" / "going to bed" / "run until done" / "be fully autonomous" → keep going.

**No is an acceptable answer.** Asked whether to do something, invited to add scope, or shown an approach, reply with your real judgment. Decline, push back, or say "this doesn't earn its place" when true. A recommendation is a judgment, not a validation. Agreement is not the default, candor over sycophancy.

The bare name `poteto-agent` errors. The chat that receives `/poteto-mode` runs the playbook. Never spawn a `poteto-agent` to run the playbook itself. Role defaults in [Models](#models), with "judgment and prose" covering prose and judgment). Code delegates tier by difficulty. The role's `@level`, or the sheet's `default effort` line, sets its starting level, and `session` starts from the session's level. Raise it one step, up to max, for the hardest or subtlest work. Lower it one step for judgment and two or more steps for routine work. Claude Code sets fast mode for the whole session, so a spawn changes only its effort. Verification is the exception and stays on the `swarm workers` model and effort (default in the **swarm** skill's Models section). Change only the effort level, and keep the model the role names, so a diverse panel stays diverse. If the model does not take that level, use its nearest level. A role on `auto` or `inherit-parent` stays on the parent model. If the `Agent` tool rejects the adjusted level, do not try another level. Use the role's line or default and say so. Never pass a rejected slug, and skip any fallback whose slug is already rejected. When the calling skill has no fallback, use the closest valid slug of the role's family from the error's list of valid slugs, or omit `model` so the subagent runs on the parent model when the list has none. **Fresh subagents by default.** Give new work to a fresh subagent with consolidated scope, meaning the original brief, every later directive, and the prior agent's report and branch. This holds for a fix round, a follow-up, a retry, and the next queue item. Resume, message, or queue a follow-up on an existing subagent only when the new work strictly needs state that lives in that agent and is costly to move: its local checkout, its uncommitted changes, or a process it still runs, such as a dev server, a simulator, or a babysit watcher. - **No long-dash character anywhere.** Write a file-list bullet as a sentence ("`main.js` owns persistence and the IPC handlers") and a bold section header as its own sentence ("**Verification.** End to end via CDP").

Comments follow the same rule as the reply. Write them clean as you go. Keep a comment only for a non-obvious *why* the code can't show. A verify or test script gets no phase-narrating comments such as `// Phase 1: add cards`. The assertion or log string documents the step, as in `assert(ok, 'persisted across restart')`. Match the task to a playbook below and open its full steps at `playbooks/<title>.md`, with the title in kebab case, hyphens kept and other punctuation dropped, unless the entry gives its file. Copy its steps in verbatim.

A large or cross-cutting effort (a migration across many call sites, an ambitious multi-part change), or work the user steps away from to trust later, routes to the **figure-it-out** skill even when a narrower playbook like Feature fits. Use **figure-it-out** whenever no bundled playbook fits. It designs a bespoke, rigorous playbook for the task. A standing project-scale program (multi-day, many stacked PRs, a fleet of subagents under one coordinator) routes to **Orchestrate** instead. figure-it-out designs one bespoke run, orchestrate runs the program.

- **Investigation.** Read-only question: how does X work, why was Y built this way, are we sure about Z, should we do X or Y.
- **Bug fix.** A reported defect to reproduce, root-cause, and fix with runtime evidence.

- **Refactoring.** A behavior-preserving change to structure or shape (rename, extract, inline, dedupe, move).

- **Authoring or modifying a skill.** Writing or editing a SKILL.md. File: `playbooks/authoring-a-skill.md`.

### Bug fix

**You own this task. Plan, review, verify.** Delegate investigation and the fix to subagents, stay in the lead. Pick each subagent's reasoning level for the job, per the Subagents section.

Be scientific. Every shipped line traces to runtime evidence. Belt-and-suspenders that "might help" is a hypothesis, not a fix. It does not ship. When evidence refutes a hypothesis, revert what it motivated. The smallest change the evidence justifies ships, nothing more.

Before the fan-out in steps 2–3, check the [focused-fix exception](#focused-fix-exception). Select known non-sensitive fields before printing diagnostic configuration or service responses; do not dump whole configurations or environments.

1. Reproduce it yourself on the matching surface via the driver skill (Non-negotiables), even when a debug or instrumentation protocol says to ask the user to reproduce. Ask the user only with a stated, specific reason the control surface cannot reach the target, and only after driving it as far as it goes. If it won't reproduce directly, synthesize the trigger, tighten conditions, or instrument until it fires.
2. Binary-search the cause. Form the candidate hypotheses, then rule them out until one survives. Seed them with `how` over the affected subsystem and the **why** skill for regression history. Each pass, take the split that cuts the most remaining problem space, get runtime evidence, eliminate. When program state is unclear, add instrumentation or logging and read it as the code runs. Don't guess. Drive a long or stubborn hunt with Claude Code's `loop` skill. Confirm the surviving *mechanism* with runtime evidence before the step-3 architect/interrogate fan-out.
3. Plan the fix. If it crosses a function boundary, `architect` first. Delegate implementation to a subagent using your configured bug-fix model (default in poteto-mode's Models section) with a specific scope.
4. Verify on the same surface. The original repro now passes. "Inconclusive" or wrong-surface is not a pass. Flag it. Unit tests show branch behavior, not bug absence.
5. Stage the commits so the failing repro lands before the fix in git history. See the **tdd** skill for the failing-test-first cadence when the bug has a cheap local test path. Skip it when the test would be expensive, integration-heavy, or unclear.
   This is the canonical **sequence-verifiable-units** principle skill, the failing test first and the fix on top.
6. Run **Opening a PR**.

For any bug fix, run `architect` in step 3 before implementing changes to interfaces, ownership, schema, migration behavior, concurrency or transaction guarantees, or deployment or routing contracts, even within one function. Before marking the fix merge-ready, require an independent correctness reviewer for changes to code that enforces a security or data-integrity invariant, including an atomic eligibility guard, even when the fix preserves that invariant. Follow the closed-review-gate rule in Subagents if a reviewer cannot run.

**Reply:** what was broken, root cause, fix, how you verified. Quote the decisive failing and passing output, trimmed to the assertion and the counts.

When publication or deployment is part of the task, also state what code was fixed and verified, what was published, what version and behavior the affected runtime actually served (through the authenticated path when relevant), and any blocker with the next action needed to resolve it. Missing or contradictory runtime evidence leaves the incident unresolved, even after a successful publication. Remove credentials and customer data from quoted evidence.

#### Focused-fix exception

One scoped bug-fix delegate may investigate the reproduced failure with a focused code and local-history read before invoking `how` or `why`. Skip those skills and step 3's `architect`, even across a function boundary, only when all of these hold:

- Runtime evidence establishes the cause in one subsystem.
- The correction preserves interfaces and state semantics, with no signature, ownership, schema, migration, security, concurrency, transaction, or deployment/routing change. Security changes include authentication, authorization, cryptography, and secret handling.
- A cheap regression check exercises the failure under the relevant runtime settings, and verification on the original surface is available.
- No competing design or contradictory evidence remains.

Record the evidence for these conditions in the existing checklist before the skip. The delegate implements the scoped fix; the lead still plans, reviews the diff, and verifies it. If any condition is false or remains unknown after the focused pass, or later evidence invalidates it, return to steps 2–3 without the exception. Every other step and any required independent review remain in force. Patch size alone never qualifies a fix.

**Goal:** connect a [Worker](/lore/workers-answer-requests-durable-objects-own-named-state) to a resource it declares, and see what it gets back.

A binding is a declared connection. On Cloudflare, it lets a Worker use a platform resource such as a bucket, a queue, or a stream. [Cloudflare bindings](https://developers.cloudflare.com/workers/runtime-apis/bindings/)
In [Alchemy](/skills/learn-alchemy), the binding is declared in the same [Effect](/lore/effect-basics) program as the resource.

## Worked example: the events cartridge writes to a stream

The events [cartridge](/lore/cartridges) sends one row per request to a Pipelines stream.
It binds the stream in two steps:

packages/events/src/basin.ts at a3f5a14861ce89913e82bea0f7ba02c83e8d4725; lines 56-57; highlighted 57. Title: Init: ask for a writer bound to the stream.

```typescript
      const saltValue = yield* salt.text;
      const writer = yield* Cloudflare.Pipelines.WriteStream(stream);
```

packages/events/src/basin.ts at a3f5a14861ce89913e82bea0f7ba02c83e8d4725; lines 75-75; highlighted none. Title: Runtime: provide the binding implementation.

```typescript
  ).pipe(Layer.provide(Cloudflare.Pipelines.WriteStreamBinding));
```

1. `Cloudflare.Pipelines.WriteStream(stream)` names the stream this code writes to. It returns a writer with a `send` method.
2. `Layer.provide(Cloudflare.Pipelines.WriteStreamBinding)` gives the [Layer](/lore/layers-make-dependencies-explicit) what it needs: it supplies the implementation that talks to the bound stream at runtime.

Alchemy documents the same two steps for queues: `WriteQueue` in the init phase, and `WriteQueueBinding` in the runtime layer. [Queue.ts](https://github.com/alchemy-run/alchemy/blob/v2.0.0-beta.85/packages/cloudflare/src/Queues/Queue.ts)

## Why a binding carries permission and configuration

Sam says a binding includes both permissions and environment variables.
A [service](/lore/services-capture-dependencies)'s configuration and permissions can be declared together before the application runs. [Happy Path 116, 37:09](https://youtu.be/YEn4A7XxgF4?t=2229) [37:33](https://youtu.be/YEn4A7XxgF4?t=2253)

He also describes deriving least-privilege policies: permissions limited to the methods an application uses. [Effect Office Hours 27, 58:16](https://youtu.be/fPSxB7ZgSJw?t=3496) [59:23](https://youtu.be/fPSxB7ZgSJw?t=3563)

## Failure it prevents

The [service](/lore/services-capture-dependencies) restarts successfully while accepted work disappears.

## Our Effect 4.0.0 reading

`Workflow`, `Activity`, and `WorkflowEngine` describe resumable work. Choose persistent engine storage. `WorkflowEngine.layerMemory` keeps state only in memory.

Source: `packages/effect/src/workflow/Workflow.ts`, `packages/effect/src/workflow/Activity.ts`, `packages/effect/src/workflow/WorkflowEngine.ts`.

Kill the worker after acceptance. Recover the same operation identity from the selected backend. This check is our proposal. The books do not prescribe it.

# Issue tracker: GitHub

Issues and specs for this repo live as GitHub issues. Use the `gh` CLI for all operations.

## Conventions

- **Create an issue**: `gh issue create --title "..." --body "..."`. Use a heredoc for multi-line bodies.
- **Read an issue**: `gh issue view <number> --json number,title,body,labels,comments`.
- **List issues**: `gh issue list --state open --json number,title,body,labels,comments --jq '[.[] | {number, title, body, labels: [.labels[].name], comments: [.comments[].body]}]'` with appropriate `--label` and `--state` filters.
- **Make an issue a sub-issue of a parent**: `gh issue create --parent <parent> ...`, or `gh issue edit <parent> --add-sub-issue <child>` afterwards (`gh` 2.94+). Older `gh`: `gh api --method POST repos/<owner>/<repo>/issues/<parent>/sub_issues -F sub_issue_id=<child-db-id>` (database id, as in **Blocking** below). Without sub-issues, put `Part of #<parent>` at the top of the child body.
- **Blocking**: GitHub's **native issue dependencies**, the canonical, UI-visible representation. Add an edge with `gh issue create --blocked-by <n>,<n> ...` or `gh issue edit <child> --add-blocked-by <blocker>` (`gh` 2.94+). Older `gh`: `gh api --method POST repos/<owner>/<repo>/issues/<child>/dependencies/blocked_by -F issue_id=<blocker-db-id>`, where `<blocker-db-id>` is the blocker's numeric **database id** (`gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/issues/<n> --jq .id`, _not_ the `#number` or `node_id`). Where dependencies aren't available, fall back to a `Blocked by: #<n>, #<n>` line at the top of the child body. A ticket is unblocked when every blocker is closed.
- **Count open blockers**: `gh api repos/<owner>/<repo>/issues/<n> --jq .issue_dependencies_summary.blocked_by` (open blockers only; 0 means startable). `gh issue view <n> --json blockedBy` also lists closed blockers, so filter it: `--jq '[.blockedBy.nodes[] | select(.state == "OPEN")] | length'`.
- **Comment on an issue**: `gh issue comment <number> --body "..."`
- **Apply / remove labels**: `gh issue edit <number> --add-label "..."` / `--remove-label "..."`
- **Close**: post the explanation with `gh issue comment <number> --body "..."`, then `gh issue close <number>`. On an already-closed issue, `gh issue close --comment` drops the comment and still exits 0.

Infer the repo from `git remote -v`; `gh` does this automatically when run inside a clone.

File issues only into the user's own repo. Never file into `mattpocock/skills` (the repo these skills come from) unless the user owns it. In a fork, `gh` can default to the upstream parent, so before the first `gh issue create` of a session, check the target with `gh repo view --json nameWithOwner` and confirm it with the user if it is not their repo.

## Pull requests as a triage surface

**PRs as a request surface: no.** _(Set to `yes` if this repo treats external PRs as feature requests; `/triage` reads this flag.)_

When set to `yes`, PRs run through the same labels and states as issues, using the `gh pr` equivalents:

Create a GitHub issue.

Used by `/wayfinder`. The **map** is a single issue with **child** issues as tickets.
